entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A casual, polite way to say no to an offer, an invitation or an optional task.
entries.usage: Common among friends, family and coworkers for food, drinks, activities or volunteering. It sounds relaxed but final; *I think I'll pass* or *I'll pass, thanks* is softer. *I'll pass on* + noun names what you are refusing: *I'll pass on the wine.*
examples: "Want to join us for karaoke tonight?" "Ha, **I'll pass**. I can't sing at all."
**I'll pass on** dessert, thanks. I'm stuffed.
"Does anyone want to take notes today?" "I think **I'll pass** this time."

drill.sentence: "We're going skydiving on Saturday. You in?" "Uh, {{I'll pass}}. I get dizzy on a ladder."
drill.hint: politely declining (two words, with *will*; not *no thanks*)

entries.related: *count me out* — firmer, often for group plans; *I'm good* — casual American way to refuse an offer; *I'll sit this one out* — skip one round or event.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: A friendly reply meaning "it's no problem" after thanks or an apology, or "don't worry about it" when you reassure someone.
entries.usage: Originally Australian, it is now very common in American speech, texts and casual emails, especially among younger people. It answers both *thank you* and *sorry*. In formal service or business settings, *You're welcome* or *Not a problem* can sound more professional.
examples: "Sorry, I forgot to bring your charger back." "**No worries**, I have another one."
"Thanks for waiting; my train was late." "**No worries**. I just got here myself."
**No worries** if you can't make it to the party; we'll catch up next week.

drill.sentence: "Oops, I think I took your seat." "Oh, {{no worries}}. I'll sit over here."
drill.hint: that's fine, relax (two words with a plural noun; not *no problem*)

entries.related: *no problem* — slightly more neutral; *it's all good* — very casual, also after apologies; *don't mention it* — a modest reply to thanks.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Tells someone they don't need to hurry; they can do it whenever it is convenient.
entries.usage: Common in speech, texts and work emails to make a request or a small debt sound relaxed. It often comes at the end of a request or as a reply to *I'll get to it soon*. *No hurry* means the same, and *There's no rush* is the full sentence.
examples: Could you look over my cover letter? **No rush**; the deadline is next month.
"Sorry, I'll pay you back for the tickets tomorrow." "**No rush**."
**There's no rush** to decide; the apartment will be available until June.

drill.sentence: Take your time finishing your breakfast, sweetie. {{No rush}}; the bus doesn't come until eight.
drill.hint: take as long as you need (two words; the noun is not *hurry* or *pressure*)

entries.related: *no hurry* — same; *no pressure* — you don't have to do it at all; *take your time* — same idea, as an instruction.

entries.label: polite request
entries.meaning: A polite add-on to a request meaning "whenever you have some free time," so the request does not sound urgent or demanding.
entries.usage: Very common in American workplace speech, emails and texts, at the start or the end of a request. It softens the request, but between coworkers it often still means "today or soon," not "whenever you like." *When you have a minute* is similar, and *at your earliest convenience* is formal and actually means "as soon as possible."
examples: Can you call me back **when you get a chance**? It's about Saturday.
**When you get a chance**, could you look at the budget I sent?
Mom, **when you get a chance**, can you text me Grandma's new address?

drill.sentence: Hey, could you water the plants {{when you get a chance}}? I'm stuck at work late.
drill.hint: whenever an opportunity comes up (five words; not *minute* or *moment*)

entries.related: *when you have a minute* — same idea; *at your convenience* — formal; *no rush* — stresses that time doesn't matter.

entries.label: closing phrase
entries.meaning: A polite way to end a phone call or conversation, presented as if you are freeing the other person to get back to their day.
entries.usage: Very common on the phone in American English, near the end of a call, and usually followed by a goodbye. It sounds considerate because it suggests the other person is busy, even when you are the one who wants to hang up. *I'll let you get back to it* is a common variant.
examples: Anyway, I know you're busy, so **I'll let you go**. Talk soon!
Well, **I'll let you go**; it sounds like the kids need you.
Okay, **I'll let you go** so you can get back to work. Thanks for the quick answer.

drill.sentence: "Sorry, the baby just woke up." "Oh, of course, {{I'll let you go}}. Call me tomorrow!"
drill.hint: a polite way to end the call (four words; not *I won't …* or *talk to you later*)

entries.related: *I won't keep you* — same idea; *I should get going* — ends the call for your own reasons; *talk to you later* — a plain goodbye.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: Says that there's no problem and the other person shouldn't worry, especially after an apology or a small mistake.
entries.usage: Casual and warm, common in American speech, especially among younger people. It often answers an apology, but it can also describe a situation that turned out fine. The short *All good* is common in texts, and both sound too casual for formal emails.
examples: "Sorry, I spilled some coffee on your table." "**It's all good**. It wipes right off."
We missed the first train, but **it's all good**; the next one's in ten minutes.
"Did the movers break anything?" "No, **it's all good**. Everything arrived in one piece."

drill.sentence: "Sorry I didn't text back last night." "{{It's all good}}, I fell asleep early anyway."
drill.hint: no problem at all (three words, starting with *it's*; very casual)

entries.related: *no worries* — same; *it's fine* — neutral, can sound cold; *no big deal* — stresses that the problem is small.

entries.label: goodbye
entries.meaning: A friendly, casual goodbye meaning "have a good day, evening or weekend," without naming the time.
entries.usage: Very common in American service encounters and with neighbors, acquaintances and coworkers at the end of a short exchange. Because *one* can stand for any period, it works at any time of day. It is friendly but not personal; with close friends, people more often say *See you* or *Take care*.
examples: "Here's your change." "Thanks, **have a good one**!"
Okay, I'm heading out. **Have a good one**, everybody.
"Thanks for fixing the sink so fast." "No problem. **Have a good one**."

drill.sentence: "That's everything, thanks." "You're welcome. {{Have a good one}}!"
drill.hint: goodbye, enjoy the rest of your day (four words; the time period isn't named)

entries.related: *have a good day* — same, names the time; *take care* — warmer; *have a nice one* — a less common variant.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says politely that you didn't hear or understand what someone just said, usually as a request to repeat it.
entries.usage: Natural on the phone, in noisy places and in meetings, often with *Sorry* in front. It puts the problem on the listener's side, so it sounds less blunt than *What?* *I didn't catch your name* is the standard way to ask for a name you missed.
examples: Sorry, **I didn't catch that**. Could you say the last part again?
The music's so loud. **I didn't catch** what you said about Saturday.
I'm sorry, **I didn't catch** your name. Was it Dana or Diana?

drill.sentence: Sorry, the connection's bad on my end. {{I didn't catch that}}. Can you repeat the address?
drill.hint: your words were lost (four words; the verb is not *hear* or *get*)

entries.related: *come again?* — very casual; *sorry?* — short, polite; *I missed that* — same idea.

entries.label: softener
entries.meaning: Shows that you are asking a question only because you are curious, not because you are criticizing or have a hidden reason.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and emails, often as *Just out of curiosity, …* before a question that might sound nosy or critical. It softens questions about choices, prices or personal matters. If the question is clearly critical, it can sound passive-aggressive.
examples: **Out of curiosity**, how much did you pay for the house?
**Just out of curiosity**, why did you switch from Python to Rust?
**Out of curiosity**, is the lake warm enough for swimming in May?

drill.sentence: {{Just out of curiosity}}, how did you two meet? You seem so different.
drill.hint: I'm only asking because I wonder (four words; not *if you don't mind me asking*)

entries.related: *if you don't mind me asking* — more careful, for personal questions; *I was just wondering* — softer, often before a request; *by the way* — changes the topic.

entries.term: if you don't mind me asking
entries.label: softener
entries.meaning: A polite softener for a personal or sensitive question, showing you know the listener might prefer not to answer.
entries.usage: Used before or after questions about age, money, health, family or the reasons for a decision. It makes the question more polite but does not make every question acceptable; very private questions can still feel intrusive. *If you don't mind my asking* is the more traditional, formal form; *me asking* is far more common in speech.
examples: **If you don't mind me asking**, what made you decide to leave medicine?
How old is your daughter now, **if you don't mind me asking**?
**If you don't mind me asking**, how much does a place like this rent for?

drill.sentence: {{If you don't mind me asking}}, why did you and your brother stop talking?
drill.hint: a polite softener for a personal question (six words; not *out of curiosity*)

entries.related: *out of curiosity* — says why you ask, less careful; *can I ask …?* — asks permission first; *if it's not too personal* — same job.

entries.label: hedging phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces something you believe is true while inviting the listener to correct you if it isn't.
entries.usage: Common in meetings, classes and discussions, usually followed by *but* and a statement or a question. It sounds modest, but speakers often use it when they are fairly sure, so it can be a polite way to challenge someone. It is more interactive than *I could be wrong*, because it asks the listener to respond.
examples: **Correct me if I'm wrong**, but isn't the store closed on Mondays?
**Correct me if I'm wrong**, but the lease says we can leave with thirty days' notice.
**Correct me if I'm wrong**, but wasn't this model trained on last year's data?

drill.sentence: {{Correct me if I'm wrong}}, but didn't we agree that your sister would host Thanksgiving this year?
drill.hint: an imperative inviting you to fix my error (not *I could be …*)

entries.related: *I could be wrong, but* — admits doubt without asking for a reply; *if I'm not mistaken* — more formal, without *but*; *unless I'm mistaken* — formal, similar.

entries.term: off the top of my head
entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Without checking facts or thinking carefully first; used when you give a quick answer from memory.
entries.usage: Very common when someone asks for a number, name or list on the spot, and it warns that the answer may be inexact or incomplete. In the negative, *I don't know off the top of my head* means "I'd have to check." It sounds natural in speech and casual emails, not in formal reports.
examples: **Off the top of my head**, I'd say the trip costs about two thousand dollars.
I don't know her number **off the top of my head**, but I can look it up.
**Off the top of my head**, the slowdown is probably in data loading, but let me check.

drill.sentence: "How many people are coming to the reunion?" "{{Off the top of my head}}, maybe forty? I'll check the list tonight."
drill.hint: without checking any records (six words; not *if I had to guess*)

entries.related: *if I had to guess* — admits you don't really know; *roughly* — approximately; *from memory* — similar, more neutral.

entries.label: hedging phrase
entries.meaning: Warns that what you just said may not be accurate, so the listener shouldn't rely on it or repeat it as fact.
entries.usage: Common in casual conversation and informal work talk after a number, a date or a rumor, and it usually follows the uncertain statement. It sounds friendly and honest rather than formal. *Don't hold me to that* is similar but is more about promises and estimates.
examples: I think the new bakery opens in May, but **don't quote me on that**.
He's supposedly moving to Austin. **Don't quote me on that**, though; I heard it from his cousin.
"When's the game?" "Seven-thirty, I think, but **don't quote me on that**."

drill.sentence: I'm pretty sure the pool closes after Labor Day, but {{don't quote me on that}}.
drill.hint: I'm not certain, so please do not repeat it as fact (not *hold me to that*)

entries.related: *don't hold me to that* — don't treat my estimate or promise as fixed; *I could be wrong* — admits doubt in advance; *last I checked* — based on older information.

entries.label: hedging phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces your best estimate while admitting that you don't really know.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, interviews and meetings when someone asks for a number, a reason or a prediction you can't be sure about. It is often followed by *I'd say*: *If I had to guess, I'd say about fifty.* It sounds honest and careful rather than vague.
examples: **If I had to guess**, I'd say there were about three hundred people at the concert.
She's upset about the seating at the wedding, not the gift, **if I had to guess**.
I haven't added up the receipts, but **if I had to guess**, we spent more on snacks than on gas.

drill.sentence: I don't know why the neighbors moved out. {{If I had to guess}}, I'd say the rent went up.
drill.hint: my best estimate, though I really don't know (a hypothetical *if*-clause)

entries.related: *my guess is* — same, a little more confident; *off the top of my head* — without checking; *I'd say* — gives a view or an estimate, less tentative.

entries.label: discourse marker
entries.meaning: Means "it is likely that"; it introduces something the speaker thinks will probably be true.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and informal writing, at the start of a sentence and followed by a clause, with or without *that*. It often predicts something about the listener: *Chances are you've seen this before.* It sounds more casual than *it's likely that* and more confident than *maybe*.
examples: If you leave after four, **chances are** you'll hit traffic on the bridge.
**Chances are** the store will have it back in stock by next week.
**Chances are** your doctor will just tell you to rest and drink lots of water.

drill.sentence: If you don't book a table now, {{chances are}} the restaurant will be full on Valentine's Day.
drill.hint: probability says (two words with a plural noun; not *odds*)

entries.related: *odds are* — same, a bit more casual; *in all likelihood* — formal; *I wouldn't be surprised if* — a cautious prediction.

entries.label: hedging phrase
entries.meaning: Says you think something is quite possible, often something negative or unexpected.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and commentary to make a prediction sound cautious. The verb after *if* is often in the past (*if they canceled*), but the present is also common in casual speech (*if they cancel*). *It wouldn't surprise me if* means the same.
examples: **I wouldn't be surprised if** they canceled the game; the field's completely flooded.
Knowing him, **I wouldn't be surprised if** he showed up late to his own wedding.
**I wouldn't be surprised if** gas prices went up again this summer.

drill.sentence: The sky is getting really dark. {{I wouldn't be surprised if}} the power went out tonight.
drill.hint: it's quite possible that (starts with *I*; not *it … me*)

entries.related: *it wouldn't surprise me if* — same; *chances are* — more confident; *I bet* — casual, stronger.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says that something is possible because the future is unpredictable, often as a reason to try, keep or prepare for something.
entries.usage: Very common in speech as a short, hopeful comment or a reason for caution. It often justifies small actions, like applying anyway, buying a lottery ticket or keeping old cables. The *you* is general: it means nobody can know.
examples: Apply anyway. **You never know**; they might love your portfolio.
I keep all my old cables in a box. **You never know** when you'll need one.
Bring a sweater. **You never know** with the weather here in May.

drill.sentence: Buy one ticket; it's only two dollars. Hey, {{you never know}}!
drill.hint: the future is unpredictable (three words: *you* + adverb + verb)

entries.related: *who knows?* — same idea, often with a shrug; *anything can happen* — stresses unpredictability; *just in case* — explains a precaution.

entries.term: when you put it that way
entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says that the other person's way of explaining something has made you see it differently, often changing your mind.
entries.usage: Common in conversation when someone reframes a choice or a problem convincingly, and it is often followed by emphatic *does*: *When you put it that way, it does sound reasonable.* With an ironic tone, it can mean the new framing makes something sound even worse. *If you put it that way* is a less common variant.
examples: "It's only three dollars a day for the gym." "Hmm, **when you put it that way**, it doesn't sound so bad."
**When you put it that way**, I guess I do owe her an apology.
"So you'd work weekends for less money?" "Okay, **when you put it that way**, it sounds terrible."

drill.sentence: "Renting a car would cost less than three taxi rides." "Huh, {{when you put it that way}}, renting makes more sense."
drill.hint: your framing changes my view (six words; not *in that case*)

entries.related: *now that you mention it* — your words made me realize something; *I never thought of it that way* — the idea is new to me; *let me put it this way* — I'll reframe it for you.

entries.term: let me put it this way
entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says you are going to explain something differently, often more bluntly or through a hint, so the listener can see the real situation.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and interviews, often after a question you don't want to answer directly; the indirect answer that follows is usually very clear. It can also introduce a simpler comparison. In casual speech, *Put it this way* alone is also common.
examples: "Was the hotel nice?" "**Let me put it this way**: we slept in the car the second night."
**Let me put it this way**: if the client sees this report, we're all in trouble.
"Is it slow?" "**Put it this way**: training that model on a laptop would take about a year."

drill.sentence: "Did your parents like your new boyfriend?" "{{Let me put it this way}}: my dad asked him to leave before dessert."
drill.hint: I'll answer indirectly but clearly (not *let's just say*)

entries.related: *let's just say* — hints without details; *to put it simply* — a simpler explanation; *put it this way* — the same, more casual.

entries.label: exclamation
entries.meaning: An exclamation meaning "that is a perfect or extreme example of …," used to comment on something that just happened.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech, followed by a noun phrase or an adjective that names the quality: *Talk about a coincidence!* or *Talk about awkward!* The tone is usually humorous, ironic or amazed; it is not a suggestion to discuss anything. It usually comes right after a short story or event.
examples: The rain started the minute we sat down for the picnic. **Talk about** bad timing!
I ran into my old roommate at a café in Tokyo. **Talk about** a small world!
She finished the marathon two months after knee surgery. **Talk about** determination.

drill.sentence: My flight got canceled, the hotel lost my reservation, and then it snowed. {{Talk about}} a bad week!
drill.hint: what an extreme example of … (an imperative of a speech verb; not *what*)

entries.related: *what a …!* — a plainer exclamation; *speaking of* — links to a topic, not an exclamation.

entries.spoken_term: you've got to be kidding me
entries.label: exclamation
entries.meaning: Expresses shock, disbelief or annoyance at something ridiculous, unfair or hard to believe.
entries.usage: Very common in casual speech, often in frustration: a canceled flight, an absurd price, a crazy suggestion. In fast speech it often sounds like *You gotta be kidding me*. It can also be a playful reply to good news you can hardly believe.
examples: Another delay? **You've got to be kidding me**. We've been here since six!
Twelve dollars for a beer? **You've got to be kidding**.
"I got the job!" "No way, **you've got to be kidding me**! Congratulations!"

drill.sentence: "The repair will cost about four thousand dollars." "Four thousand? {{You've got to be kidding me}}!"
drill.hint: this is ridiculous, I can't believe it (six words; not *are you serious*)

entries.related: *are you serious?* — similar, a real question; *no way!* — surprise, often positive; *you must be joking* — same idea.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: A reply that agrees strongly and happily with what someone just said, as if they had read your mind.
entries.usage: Very common in casual American speech and texting, especially among younger speakers, with the stress on *right*. It shows enthusiastic shared feeling about something surprising, funny or annoying. It sounds too casual for formal settings.
examples: "This ramen is amazing." "**I know, right?** I've been coming here for years."
"Can you believe how expensive concert tickets are now?" "**I know, right?** It's insane."
"That plot twist was wild." "**I know, right?** I did not see that coming."

drill.sentence: "Their new baby is so cute!" "{{I know, right?}} I could look at her pictures all day."
drill.hint: I totally agree (a casual three-word reply ending in a question mark)

entries.related: *right?* — shorter, same; *tell me about it* — agreement about something bad; *totally* — simple agreement.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says that a situation can't be changed, so you accept it, often with some disappointment.
entries.usage: Very common in American speech, sports interviews and workplace talk; it sounds calm and resigned, and it often closes a complaint. Some people find it dismissive, because it can sound like refusing to look for solutions.
examples: Our flight's delayed three hours. **It is what it is**; let's get some food.
The coach said the loss hurt, but **it is what it is**, and they'll be back next season.
I wish I'd gotten the bigger office, but **it is what it is**.

drill.sentence: "You're stuck working on Christmas?" "Yeah. {{It is what it is}}. At least it's double pay."
drill.hint: I can't change it, so I accept it (five words; not *such is life*)

entries.related: *oh well* — lighter; *what can you do?* — resigned, often humorous; *such is life* — similar, a bit literary.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Used when handing something to someone (*here you are*), when praising someone who has just done it right (*that's right*), or when ending an explanation with a shrug (*that's how it is*).
entries.usage: Very common in casual speech, and the situation decides the meaning: cashiers say it when handing over change, coaches and teachers say it as encouragement, and in conversation *So there you go* closes a point. *There you are* is a slightly more formal way to hand something over. *There you go again* is different: it complains that someone is repeating an annoying habit.
examples: "Can I get a large coffee?" "Sure. **There you go**; that's three fifty."
Lift with your legs, not your back. **There you go**, perfect.
He worked hard, saved every penny and bought a house at thirty. So **there you go**.

drill.sentence: "Is this how you hold the racket?" "{{There you go}}! Now just swing a little later."
drill.hint: encouragement: that's exactly right (three words; not *that's it* or *you've got it*)

entries.related: *here you go* — when handing something over; *that's it* — encouragement, same; *there you have it* — ends an explanation or a summary.

entries.label: spoken tag
entries.meaning: A tag at the end of an explanation that checks whether the listener has followed you and often softens what you said.
entries.usage: Very common in American speech, especially in meetings, teaching and interviews; it sounds modest and considerate. Unlike the question *Does that make sense?*, it usually doesn't wait for an answer. Used after every point, it can make you sound unsure of yourself.
examples: I'd rather clean on Saturdays so the weekdays stay free, **if that makes sense**.
We should test the small version first and only then scale up, **if that makes sense**.
I love her, but I need a little space from her right now, **if that makes sense**.

drill.sentence: I want to see my friends more, but on my own terms, {{if that makes sense}}.
drill.hint: if you follow my reasoning (a four-word tag; not *if you know what I mean*)

entries.related: *does that make sense?* — a real question; *if you know what I mean* — hints at something not fully said; *you know?* — very casual.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Means "honestly"; it introduces a frank admission, often about a feeling the speaker is a little embarrassed by.
entries.usage: Very common in casual American speech and online, especially among younger speakers. Despite the words, what follows is usually a harmless admission, not the confession of a real lie. In texts it is often *Not gonna lie* or *NGL*.
examples: **I'm not gonna lie**, I cried at the end of that dog movie.
I was nervous about meeting her parents, **I'm not gonna lie**.
**Not gonna lie**, the new office coffee is way better than I expected.

drill.sentence: {{I'm not gonna lie}}, I ate the whole bag of chips while watching the game.
drill.hint: a very casual frank admission — literally, a promise not to deceive (four words)

entries.related: *to be honest* — neutral; *if I'm being honest* — more personal; *I'll admit* — concedes something.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces information you think the listener should have, often a warning or something they might not like.
entries.usage: Common in speech, texts and casual emails, usually at the start of the sentence. It sounds friendly and helpful, but with a sharp tone it can sound defensive or pointed. *FYI* is the common written shorthand.
examples: **Just so you know**, the front door sticks, so pull it hard.
I'll be out of the office on Friday, **just so you know**.
**Just so you know**, I wasn't the one who told her about the party.

drill.sentence: {{Just so you know}}, the dog jumps on guests, so maybe don't wear white pants.
drill.hint: a friendly advance warning (four words; not *heads up*)

entries.related: *heads up* — a quick warning; *for your information* — can sound sharp in speech; *just to let you know* — same, slightly more neutral.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces a statement or a checking question meant to prevent any misunderstanding.
entries.usage: Common in meetings, negotiations, emails and serious personal talks. It can sound firm or even sharp, especially when stating limits: *Just to be clear, I'm not paying for this.* It also introduces a question that checks an arrangement.
examples: **Just to be clear**, I'm not angry; I just want to understand what happened.
So, **just to be clear**, the deposit is non-refundable, right?
And **just to be clear**: this is the last time I'm lending you my car.

drill.sentence: {{Just to be clear}}, you're picking up the kids today, and I'm doing it tomorrow?
drill.hint: so we don't misunderstand each other (four words, with an infinitive; not *to clarify*)

entries.related: *to clarify* — more formal; *let me get this straight* — checks something surprising, can sound annoyed; *for the record* — states something so it is noted.

entries.label: discourse marker
entries.meaning: Says that after thinking again, you have changed your mind about something you just said or decided.
entries.usage: Common in speech and informal writing, usually right before the new decision. American English uses the singular; British speakers usually say *on second thoughts*. It often reverses a choice made seconds earlier, so it can sound spontaneous or funny.
examples: I'll have the burger. Actually, **on second thought**, make it the salad.
**On second thought**, let's not tell Mom about the dent until after dinner.
We were going to drive, but **on second thought**, the train is faster at rush hour.

drill.sentence: Sure, I'll come to the party. Wait, {{on second thought}}, I'd better not; I have an early flight.
drill.hint: after reconsidering, I'm changing my mind (three words; not *actually*)

entries.related: *come to think of it* — a sudden realization, not always a change of mind; *then again* — adds a doubt; *scratch that* — cancels what you just said.

entries.label: polite advice
entries.meaning: A polite, indirect way to give advice or a warning; it means "I suggest that you" or "you should."
entries.usage: Very common in American speech and work emails because it sounds less bossy than *you should*; *you may want to* is a bit more formal. It is often used for tactful corrections and warnings. With a serious tone it can be quite firm, almost an instruction.
examples: **You might want to** bring a jacket; it gets cold by the lake at night.
Before you send it, **you might want to** double-check the client's name.
Um, **you might want to** check your teeth. There's some spinach in there.

drill.sentence: The roads are icy tonight, so {{you might want to}} leave a little earlier than usual.
drill.hint: a polite, indirect *you should* (four words; not *may*)

entries.related: *you should* — direct advice; *you'd better* — stronger, a warning; *it might be worth* + *-ing* — a very polite suggestion.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: Says that you have everything you need or are ready, usually in reply to an offer of help.
entries.usage: Very common in American service situations: it politely declines more help, and servers ask *Are you all set?* to check if a customer is finished or ready to pay. It can also mean "ready to go": *Are we all set for tomorrow?*
examples: "Do you need a bag?" "No, **I'm all set**, thanks."
"Need help with your suitcase?" "Thanks, but **I'm all set**."
Tickets, passports, snacks: **we're all set** for the road trip.

drill.sentence: "Want me to iron a shirt for your interview?" "No thanks, {{I'm all set}} for tomorrow. I did it last night."
drill.hint: fully prepared (three words; not *… good* or *… ready*)

entries.related: *I'm good* — casual, same in offers; *I'm fine, thanks* — neutral; *all set?* — a server's question meaning "ready?" or "finished?"

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says that you can handle a task yourself without help, or that you will pay the bill.
entries.usage: Common among friends, family and coworkers; when paying, people say it while reaching for the check. Said to someone offering help, it sounds confident, but repeated too often it can sound stubborn. In fast speech it is often *I got this*.
examples: Put your wallet away; **I've got this**. You paid last time.
"Want me to call the landlord?" "No, **I've got this**. I'll call him tonight."
Go home and rest. **I've got this**, and I'll text you when the kids are asleep.

drill.sentence: "Let's split the bill." "No way, {{I've got this}}. It's your birthday."
drill.hint: I'll pay (three words, present perfect, ending in a demonstrative; not *it's on me*)

entries.related: *it's on me* — I'm paying; *my treat* — I'm paying, warmer; *you've got this* — encouragement for someone else.

entries.label: encouragement
entries.meaning: Encourages someone before a challenge: "you can do it; I believe in you."
entries.usage: Very common in American speech, texts and social media before exams, interviews, races or hard conversations. It is warm and supportive, used by friends, family, coaches and coworkers. In texts it is often written *You got this*.
examples: Nervous about asking for a raise? **You've got this**. You've more than earned it.
Before my son's first solo hike up the mountain, I texted him, "**You've got this**. Call me from the top."
At mile twenty-three, strangers on the sidewalk kept shouting, "**You've got this**!"

drill.sentence: I know the bar exam is scary, but you studied for months. {{You've got this}}!
drill.hint: I believe in you (three words, present perfect; not *you can do it*)

entries.related: *you can do it* — plainer; *break a leg* — good luck before a performance; *I've got this* — I can handle it myself.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Means "I would really like" or "I really need" something, often to feel better or to get through a situation.
entries.usage: Common in casual American speech and followed by a noun: *a drink*, *some help*, *a vacation*. It sounds understated, so *I could really use a break* expresses a strong need politely. It also works in offers (*Could you use a hand?*), and British speakers often say *I could do with* instead.
examples: It's been a long week. **I could use** a drink.
If you're free on Saturday, **I could use** some help moving the couch.
You look exhausted. You **could use** a vacation.

drill.sentence: I've been cleaning out the garage all morning. {{I could use}} a cold drink.
drill.hint: I'd really like (understated; three words; not *I need* or *I'd love*)

entries.related: *I could go for* — I'd like to eat or do this; *I could do with* — same, more British; *I need* — more direct.

entries.label: understatement
entries.meaning: An understated way of saying "no" or "not really," usually as a contrast with something that does apply.
entries.usage: Common in casual American speech and often humorous, typically after a contrast: *The food was great; the service, not so much.* It can also be a short reply on its own. The tone is light, so it works for gentle criticism or a polite *no*.
examples: I love living here. The winters, **not so much**.
"Did you enjoy the camping trip?" "The hiking was great. The mosquitoes, **not so much**."
"Are you a morning person?" "Um, **not so much**."

drill.sentence: My son loves soccer; homework, {{not so much}}.
drill.hint: a light, understated *no* (three words; not *not really* or *not at all*)

entries.related: *not really* — a plain, polite *no*; *not exactly* — ironic, "not at all"; *not a fan* — casual dislike.

entries.label: discourse marker
entries.meaning: Admits that something is true before you make a stronger, contrasting point; it means "admittedly."
entries.usage: Common in conversation, opinion writing and debate. It usually starts the sentence and is followed by *but* in the same or the next sentence. *Admittedly* is the more formal equivalent.
examples: **Granted**, the apartment is small, but you can't beat the location.
He's not the fastest player on the team, **granted**, but nobody works harder.
**Granted**, the sample is small, but the effect showed up in every group we tested.

drill.sentence: {{Granted}}, the hike is long and steep, but the view from the top is worth every step.
drill.hint: I accept this is true (one word, a past participle; not *admittedly*)

entries.related: *admittedly* — same, more formal; *I'll give you that* — concedes a point, usually after it; *sure, but* — a casual concession.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces something that happened suddenly and surprisingly soon after, often in a story.
entries.usage: Typical of casual storytelling; it speeds up the story and stresses surprise. It is often followed by the present tense, as if the story is happening now, but the past also works. *The next thing I knew* is the past version for your own experience.
examples: We started chatting on the train, and **next thing you know**, we're planning a trip together.
He bought one little plant in March. **Next thing you know**, the apartment's a jungle.
Give a toddler your phone once, and **next thing you know**, they're asking for it every day.

drill.sentence: My cousin went to Lisbon for one week, and {{next thing you know}}, she's buying a house there.
drill.hint: suddenly, surprisingly soon after (four words, general *you*; not *before …*)

entries.related: *before you know it* — soon, usually about the future; *the next thing I knew* — personal, past; *all of a sudden* — suddenly, neutral.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says that something is a safe, reliable choice that will always be good.
entries.usage: Common in recommendations about food, gifts, clothes, places and music; it sounds friendly and confident. It is followed by a noun or an *-ing* form. *You can't go wrong* can also stand alone after a list of options.
entries.pattern: you can't go wrong with + noun / -ing
examples: If you don't know what to get her, **you can't go wrong with** flowers.
For a first trip to Italy, **you can't go wrong with** Rome and Florence.
"Which ice cream should we get?" "**You can't go wrong with** chocolate."

drill.sentence: If you're cooking for picky eaters, {{you can't go wrong with}} spaghetti and meatballs.
drill.hint: it's always a safe choice (five words, ending in *with*)

entries.related: *a safe bet* — a choice that is likely to work; *stick with* — keep choosing something reliable; *a crowd-pleaser* — something most people like.

entries.label: discourse marker
entries.meaning: Moves to a new topic or ends a conversation, linking the move to what was just said.
entries.usage: Common in meetings, speeches and conversation, especially to end things: *On that note, let's call it a day.* After a sad or awkward comment, people use it humorously to escape, often with an ironic adjective: *on that cheerful note*. *On a related note* adds a connected point instead of closing.
examples: So we all agree on the budget. **On that note**, let's wrap up and get lunch.
"The vet bill came to nine hundred dollars." "Well, **on that** cheerful **note**, let's get the check."
The kids are finally asleep. **On that note**, who wants a glass of wine?

drill.sentence: "We still have a four-hour drive tomorrow." "Right. {{On that note}}, I'm heading to bed."
drill.hint: linking to what was just said, to end the chat (three words; not *with that*)

entries.related: *with that* — ends a speech or a meeting; *speaking of which* — moves to a related topic; *on a related note* — adds a connected point.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Admits that the other person is right about one particular point, while you keep your overall view.
entries.usage: Common in friendly arguments and debates, usually right after the point you concede, and often followed by *but*. It sounds fair-minded and a little reluctant. *I'll grant you that* is similar and slightly more formal.
examples: Okay, the food was good, **I'll give you that**. But the service was terrible.
She's a great speaker, **I'll give you that**, but her plan doesn't add up.
"At least the new phone has better battery life." "True, **I'll give you that**."

drill.sentence: "Come on, the view from the balcony was incredible." "Okay, {{I'll give you that}}. But the room itself was tiny."
drill.hint: I concede that one point (four words; not *grant*)

entries.related: *granted* — concedes before the main point; *fair point* — admits a good argument; *you have a point* — you're partly right.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: Says that the other person is right, often reluctantly or with a touch of humor.
entries.usage: Common in casual conversation; the understatement can sound grudging (*Ugh, you're not wrong*), dry, or simply warm. It is often used when the truth is a little uncomfortable for the speaker. *You're right* is plainer and fully open.
examples: "You've been working too much lately." "Ugh, **you're not wrong**."
"This apartment is way too small for two dogs." "Yeah, **you're not wrong**."
"We spent more on takeout than groceries this month." "**You're not wrong**, and it has to stop."

drill.sentence: "Your brother always shows up when there's free food." "Ha, {{you're not wrong}}."
drill.hint: that's right — a grudging understatement (three words, with a negative)

entries.related: *you're right* — plain agreement; *fair point* — admits a good argument; *you have a point* — partly right.

entries.label: spoken question
entries.meaning: A short question asking someone to explain what they mean, or in what way their statement is true.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, meetings and interviews. It is brief and neutral, so it invites an explanation without sounding hostile, although a sharp tone can make it a challenge. It follows a claim or an opinion, not a simple fact.
examples: "I think the new schedule is going to backfire." "**How so?**"
"Moving to Denver changed my life." "Really? **How so?**"
"That contract is worse than it looks." "**How so?** It seemed pretty standard to me."

drill.sentence: "Honestly, the cheaper car will cost us more in the long run." "{{How so?}} It gets better gas mileage."
drill.hint: in what way? please explain (two words; the second is an adverb)

entries.related: *what do you mean?* — fuller, sometimes defensive; *how come?* — asks why, not in what way; *in what way?* — more formal.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Signals that you are repeating a point you already made.
entries.usage: Very common in speech; it can be neutral or impatient, suggesting the listener wasn't paying attention. *As I said* is the more formal version and is preferred in careful writing. Used too often, it can sound defensive.
examples: **Like I said**, I'm happy to help, but I can't do Saturday.
**Like I said** on the phone, the leak is coming from the upstairs bathroom.
I didn't take your charger, **like I said**. Check your car.

drill.sentence: {{Like I said}}, the kids need to be picked up at three, not three-thirty.
drill.hint: repeating what I mentioned before (casual, three words; not *as …*)

entries.related: *as I said* — more formal; *as I mentioned* — polite, good in emails; *again* — short, can sound impatient.

entries.label: polite request
entries.meaning: A casual, polite way to ask a favor; it means "would it be possible for you to …?"
entries.usage: Common in speech, texts and casual work emails for small favors from friends and coworkers. It suggests the person can easily say no, so it sounds less demanding than *Can you …?* The full form *Is there any chance you could …?* is a bit more polite.
examples: **Any chance you could** pick me up from the airport on Friday?
Hey, **any chance you could** cover my shift tomorrow? I'll take yours next week.
**Any chance you could** send me those photos from the wedding?

drill.sentence: {{Any chance you could}} feed my cat this weekend? I'm visiting my parents.
drill.hint: a casual favor request (four words; not *any way you could*)

entries.related: *could you possibly …?* — more formal; *would you mind …?* — polite, followed by *-ing*; *do you think you could …?* — polite and tentative.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: Says that you agree with the other person on a particular point.
entries.usage: Common in casual conversation and meetings; *on that* limits the agreement to one point, and *I'm with you there* means the same. *I'm with you* alone can also mean "I support you" or "I follow what you're saying." It often comes before a *but* that adds a different view on another point.
examples: "The new bus schedule is terrible." "Oh, **I'm with you on that**."
**I'm with you on** the price, but I still think the location matters more.
"We should leave before the traffic starts." "**I'm with you**. Let's go."

drill.sentence: "Christmas music shouldn't start before Thanksgiving." "Finally, someone said it! {{I'm with you on that}}."
drill.hint: I agree on this point (five words, with a preposition of company)

entries.related: *I agree* — neutral; *that makes two of us* — I feel or think the same about myself; *you're telling me* — strong agreement about something bad.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: Shows strong agreement, as if to say "I know that even better than you do," usually about something difficult or annoying.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech, with the stress on *me*. It often comes from someone directly affected, like a commuter hearing that traffic is bad. It is friendly between people who share a problem, but it can sound dismissive if it turns someone's complaint into your own.
examples: "Your son has so much energy." "**You're telling me**. He was up at five this morning."
"It's freezing in this office." "**You're telling me**; my desk is right under the vent."
"Rent in this city is crazy." "**You're telling me**. Mine went up four hundred dollars."

drill.sentence: "Your neighbor's dog barks a lot." "{{You're telling me}}! I hear it every night at two."
drill.hint: I know that far better than you do (three words; not *tell me about it* or *no kidding*)

entries.related: *tell me about it* — same, about shared experience; *I'm telling you* — insists the listener believe you; *no kidding* — agreement with the obvious, can be sarcastic.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: A reply saying that you feel the same, think the same, or are in the same situation as the speaker.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech as a reply to a statement about the speaker's own feelings or situation, often with humor or shared frustration. It does not fit as agreement with a general claim; for that, say *I agree* or *I'm with you on that*.
examples: "I have no idea what the teacher was talking about." "**That makes two of us**."
"I'm starving." "**That makes two of us**. Let's order."
"I can't wait for this week to be over." "Ha, **that makes two of us**."

drill.sentence: "I'm so nervous about the wedding speech." "{{That makes two of us}}. I've rewritten mine six times."
drill.hint: you're not alone in this feeling (five words; not *me too* or *same here*)

entries.related: *me too* — plain; *same here* — casual; *welcome to the club* — you're in the same bad situation as many others.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: Says that you accept someone's criticism or argument, often briefly and without arguing back.
entries.usage: Common in meetings, discussions and emails; it can sound gracious, or a little curt if said flatly, as if to end the topic. *I take your point* is the fuller, more formal version and is often followed by *but*.
examples: "Your emails are really long." "**Point taken**. I'll keep them shorter."
"We can't afford a trip to Hawaii and a new couch." "Okay, **point taken**."
"You keep interrupting her." "**Point taken**. Sorry, go ahead."

drill.sentence: "If you keep buying lunch every day, you'll never save for the trip." "Okay, okay, {{point taken}}. I'll start packing sandwiches."
drill.hint: I accept your criticism (noun + past participle; not *message received*)

entries.related: *fair point* — admits the argument is good; *that's fair* — accepts criticism, warmer; *noted* — very short, can sound cold.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says that you understand someone's situation, feeling or reason, often before you disagree or say no.
entries.usage: Very common in American speech; it sounds sympathetic but usually prepares a *but*. It can stand alone or be followed by a clause: *I get that you're tired, but …* Said flatly and too often, it can sound dismissive.
examples: **I get that** you're busy, but we promised your mom we'd come.
"I can't afford to go out this week." "Totally, **I get that**."
**I get that** money is tight, but we can't keep putting off the roof repair.

drill.sentence: {{I get that}} you're nervous about the surgery, but the doctor does this every day.
drill.hint: a sympathetic acknowledgment (three words, casual verb; not *I know that* or *I realize that*)

entries.related: *I hear you* — sympathetic, often about feelings; *I understand* — more formal; *I see where you're coming from* — understands the reasons behind a view.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: Strongly agrees by saying the other person has just stated your own point: "exactly, that's my point too."
entries.usage: Common in casual American speech, often excited or a little triumphant, when someone finally sees your point or arrives at it on their own. The stress usually falls on *saying*. It can also mean you are repeating your point because someone missed it.
examples: "We should just rent a cabin instead of a hotel." "**That's what I'm saying**! It's cheaper and way more fun."
"The team really needs a better goalie." "**That's what I'm saying**! Nobody listens to me."
"Maybe the problem isn't the recipe; maybe it's the oven." "Yes! **That's what I'm saying**."

drill.sentence: "Honestly, the coffee here is better than at that fancy place." "{{That's what I'm saying}}! And it's half the price."
drill.hint: exactly, you've stated my point (four words, present progressive)

entries.related: *exactly* — plain agreement; *I know, right?* — happy agreement about a feeling; *like I said* — repeats your earlier point.
